summary: Isaiah 10 (34 verses) continues the story of holiness. Starting with 'Woe to those who decree unrighteous decrees, and to the writers who write oppressive decrees', it moves through themes of holiness, judgment and calls readers toward hope.
whyItMatters: This chapter matters because it shows holiness lived out in assyrian crisis, exile hope. For a first-time reader, it answers: who is God in this moment, what does he ask, and how do people respond.

keyVerses.text: Woe to those who decree unrighteous decrees, and to the writers who write oppressive decrees
He will consume the glory of his forest and of his fruitful field, both soul and body. It will be as when a standard bearer faints.
He will cut down the thickets of the forest with iron, and Lebanon will fall by the Mighty One.

questions.question: What is happening in Isaiah 10?
questions.answer: In 34 verses, this chapter isaiah 10 (34 verses) continues the story of holiness. starting with 'woe to those who decree unrighteous decrees, and to the writers who write oppressive decrees', it moves through themes of holiness, judgment and calls readers toward hope. The setting is assyrian crisis, exile hope, written to judah. Look for who speaks, who listens, and what changes by the end.

questions.question: Who wrote Isaiah and why 10 matters in the bigger story?
questions.answer: Traditionally isaiah son of amoz, addressed to judah around ~700 bc. This chapter fits the book's purpose as prophecy — its themes of holiness, judgment build on what came before.

questions.question: What does 'righteousness' mean in this chapter?
questions.answer: Being in right standing, doing what is right. In this chapter, it appears in context of holiness. For a first-time reader: think of it as being in right standing, doing what is right, not just religious jargon.

questions.question: What does this chapter teach about God or people?
questions.answer: Through holiness and judgment, it shows God's character (faithful, just, merciful) and human tendency (need, failure, hope). Notice how verses move from problem to provision.

questions.question: Verse 13 is long — what is it saying in plain English?
questions.answer: The verse says: 'For he has said, “By the strength of my hand I have done it, and by my wisdom, for I have understanding. I have removed the boundaries of the peoples, and have robbed their treasur...' In plain terms: it is making a key point about holiness. Break it into two halves — what is described, and what is promised or commanded.

questions.question: How could this chapter apply today without forcing modern ideas onto it?
questions.answer: Ask: what was original audience supposed to do with this? Then ask: what similar situation exists today? For example, if chapter warns about idols, today that might be money or status; if it celebrates deliverance, where do people need deliverance today?
